title: Dentistry — A carer asking about mouth care in dementia
before:
Ask her to describe exactly what happens when she tries, at what time of day, and what her mother
does.

Say clearly and kindly that holding her mother's chin and forcing the brush is not something to
continue, and explain what it does — the distress, the risk of injury, and that it makes the next
attempt harder.

Acknowledge that she has been trying to do the right thing with no help and no training, and say so
before offering any correction.

Give the practical techniques: approaching from the side rather than the front, a small-headed or
child's brush, doing it at the time of day her mother is calmest, letting her hold the brush too,
brushing alongside her, and stopping and returning later.

Explain what matters most if only a little can be achieved: the fluoride staying in contact rather
than a perfect clean, a non-foaming or high-fluoride paste, and not rinsing afterwards.

Ask what her mother's mouth looks like, whether she is eating, whether she holds her face, and
whether anyone has looked in her mouth recently.

Explain what you can do: a domiciliary visit or an appointment here, and what would happen at it.

Ask how she herself is managing, and mention the carers' support that exists.

Agree what she will try this week and arrange the assessment before she leaves.
